For a fleet of old laptops and repurposed phones running Ubuntu 26.04, the best free distributed SQL option is rqlite (or dqlite). Enterprise distributed SQL databases like CockroachDB or YugabyteDB require heavy RAM and CPU that will overwhelm older hardware or mobile architectures.

Why Lightweight Distributed SQL is Best Here

Low Memory Footprint: Built on SQLite, these options consume only tens of megabytes of RAM.

Mixed Architecture Support: Easily compiles or runs across x86 old laptops and ARM-based repurposed phones.

Fault Tolerance: Uses consensus protocols to keep data synchronized even if older devices drop offline unpredictably. [1]

Top Recommendations

rqlite

What it is: Lightweight, distributed relational database built on SQLite using the Raft consensus protocol.

Pros: Single tiny binary, exposes a simple HTTP/JSON API as well as standard SQL drivers, trivial to spin up on mixed Linux/Ubuntu nodes.

Cons: Write throughput is limited by consensus overhead and underlying SQLite constraints, making it poor for heavy write-intensive logging. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

dqlite (Distributed SQLite)

What it is: C-based embeddable distributed SQL database created by Canonical (the makers of Ubuntu).

Pros: Extremely fast, near-zero overhead, designed specifically for native clustering on Ubuntu environments.

Cons: Requires more custom application integration compared to a standalone server daemon like rqlite. [1, 2]

LibSQL / Turso (Self-Hosted)

What it is: An open-source fork of SQLite optimized for edge and distributed replication. Turso is the managed database-as-a-service (DBaaS) built on LibSQL, designed to provide a globally distributed, low-latency data layer for edge applications.

Pros: Great for edge synchronization patterns across sporadic network connections.

Cons: Slightly more complex operational topology for a multi-node ad-hoc local cluster.

Deployment Tips for Old Hardware

Watch the SD/Disk Wear: Repurposed phones and old laptop HDDs/SSDs have degraded write endurance. Mount your database directory with commit intervals or journaling modes tuned to minimize heavy disk thrashing.

Network Flakiness: Old Wi-Fi cards and mobile batteries mean nodes will drop. Configure generous heartbeat and election timeouts in your Raft/consensus configuration to prevent constant leader.

## What the paper actually establishes

This is more interesting for us than the headline, but in a different way than “we only need one transformer layer.”

The experiment still runs the **entire pretrained transformer**. All layers participate in the forward pass, and gradients are backpropagated through the full network. The intervention is that **only one selected transformer's parameters are allowed to update**; embeddings, head, and every other layer are frozen. 

So:

> **One layer is enough to absorb much of the RL adaptation.  
> One layer is not enough to perform inference.**

That distinction is load-bearing.

Across seven models from 1.5B–8B, including Qwen3, Qwen2.5 and a DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen model, using three RL algorithms and math, coding and agentic tasks, the authors found the same basic structure: **high-contribution layers cluster around the middle of the transformer stack.** In every tested model, the best single layer matched or exceeded the gain from full-parameter RL.  

And it is not merely a funny ablation result. When they trained only the best 5 or 10 layers, those selective configurations **beat full-parameter RL** on their tested Qwen3 scales. Even simply choosing middle layers by position—without doing an expensive layer-by-layer census first—was a strong heuristic.  

There is another result that interests me even more for DE. Different high-contribution single-layer variants learned **different useful behaviors**. On their OlympiadBench experiment, the newly solved problem sets overlapped only modestly; an ensemble of the layer-specialized variants beat both the best individual variant and the ordinary full-RL model. 

That looks like genuine structural diversity, not merely “make the same model seven times.”

This paper lands directly on one of the most interesting hypotheses already developing inside Priority AI:

That is evidence of non-uniform functional plasticity within transformer depth.

It is NOT evidence that “one layer is all an LLM needs.”
It is NOT evidence that single-layer inference works.
It is NOT evidence that we can arbitrarily assign one physical machine per layer.
It is NOT yet evidence that this result transfers to our Qwen3.5-4B target.
It is specifically evidence about RL post-training.

1. LAYER-WISE INFERENCE
